prompt.english:
Which animal do you need help with?

1. Cow
2. Poultry
3. Pig
4. Rabbit
5. Goat
6. Sheep
7. Dog

Cattle — what do you need help with?

1. Feed & Nutrition
2. Disease Prevention
3. Tick Control
4. Breeds & Breeding

Poultry — what do you need help with?

1. Feed & Nutrition
2. General Care
3. Breeds

Pigs — what do you need help with?

1. Feed & Nutrition
2. Disease Prevention
3. Breeds & Breeding

Rabbits — what do you need help with?

1. Feed & Nutrition
2. Disease Prevention
3. Breeds & Breeding

Goats — what do you need help with?

1. Feed & Nutrition
2. General Care
3. Disease Prevention
4. Tick Control
5. Breeds & Breeding

Sheep — what do you need help with?

1. Feed & Nutrition
2. General Care
3. Disease Prevention
4. Tick Control
5. Breeds & Breeding

Dogs — what do you need help with?

1. General Care & Feeding
2. Disease Prevention
3. Breeding

Cattle Feed (1/5)
Cattle need forage like grass and hay
for a balanced diet.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Feed (2/5)
Allow 6-8 hours of grazing per day.
Provide clean fresh water at all times
— always available, not just 4x daily.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Feed (3/5)
Napier Grass is best for dairy and
beef cattle. High yield, drought
resistant. Requires regular pruning.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Feed (4/5)
In dry season, use Maize Stover as
roughage. Low in nutrients alone —
combine with other feeds.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Feed (5/5)
Dairy Meal Concentrates boost milk
yield. Leguminous Shrubs add protein
— especially good for lactating cows.
1. Back to menu

Cattle Prevention (1/6)
Control ticks regularly. Ticks spread
East Coast Fever, Anaplasmosis,
Babesiosis and Heartwater.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Prevention (2/6)
Vaccinate animals on a
vet-recommended schedule.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Prevention (3/6)
Isolate any cow that aborts for
at least 3 weeks.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Prevention (4/6)
Keep udders clean before and
after milking.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Prevention (5/6)
Milk sick cows last to avoid
spreading infection — especially
important for mastitis.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Prevention (6/6)
Dispose of contaminated materials
safely — birth fluids, dead calves.
1. Back to menu

Cattle Tick Control (1/3)
Ticks spread East Coast Fever,
Anaplasmosis, Babesiosis and
Heartwater. Control is essential.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Tick Control (2/3)
Dip or spray cattle regularly with
acaricides. Follow the recommended
schedule from your vet.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Tick Control (3/3)
Check animals regularly for ticks
especially around ears, legs and
under the tail.
1. Back to menu

Cattle Breeds (1/5)
Ankole and Zebu — adapted to local
environment. Good for milk and meat.
Easy to manage but lower milk yield.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Breeds (2/5)
Friesian x Ankole cross improves
milk production.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Breeds (3/5)
Boran x Ankole cross improves meat
quality and keeps disease resistance.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Breeds (4/5)
Artificial Insemination (AI)
introduces superior genetics to
improve milk or meat productivity.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Cattle Breeds (5/5)
Selective Breeding — choose stock
based on desired traits like milk
yield or growth rate.
1. Back to menu

Poultry Feed (1/4)
Energy foods: corn, sorghum,
milling by-products.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Poultry Feed (2/4)
Protein foods: soybean meal,
fishmeal, groundnuts, cottonseed
meal, beans, field peas.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Poultry Feed (3/4)
Vitamin supplements: banana leaves,
yam leaves, alfalfa, fish oil
(provides vitamins A and D), yeast.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Poultry Feed (4/4)
Mineral supplements: meat and bone
meal, fishmeal, seaweed (kelp).
1. Back to menu

Poultry Care (1/3)
Keep housing clean, dry,
well-ventilated and spacious.
Feed according to age and type —
layers and broilers need different diets.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Poultry Care (2/3)
Check birds every day for signs of
illness or injury. Vaccinate on a
vet-recommended schedule.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Poultry Care (3/3)
Use biosecurity — limit who enters
the poultry area. Handle birds
gently to reduce stress.
1. Back to menu

Poultry Breeds (1/2)
Egg Layers: Lehman Brown, Gold Brown,
Harvard White, Bovanche White,
ISA White.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Poultry Breeds (2/2)
Meat Breeds: Broilers Type 1 & 2,
Kuroilers.
1. Back to menu

Pig Feed (1/2)
Protein: soybean meal, fishmeal,
groundnuts, brewers spent grain.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Pig Feed (2/2)
Energy: cassava, maize/corn, sweet
potato vines, rice bran.
1. Back to menu

Pig Prevention (1/5)
Strict biosecurity — limit visitors
to pig area. Avoid contact between
your pigs and wild pigs (ASF risk).
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Pig Prevention (2/5)
Vaccinate against Foot and Mouth
Disease and Swine Erysipelas.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Pig Prevention (3/5)
Clean housing regularly. Control
rodents — rats spread Swine
Dysentery. Avoid overcrowding.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Pig Prevention (4/5)
Deworm pigs every 3-6 months.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Pig Prevention (5/5)
Dispose of pig feces properly.
1. Back to menu

Pig Breeds (1/2)
Large White (Yorkshire), Landrace,
Duroc, Hampshire, Local/Indigenous.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Pig Breeds (2/2)
Select healthy strong animals for
breeding. Ensure breeding pigs get
adequate nutrition — especially protein.
Monitor sows during gestation.
1. Back to menu

Rabbit Feed (1/3)
Main diet: grass and hay (Timothy,
Bermuda, alfalfa). Provides fiber to
prevent gut blockages.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Rabbit Feed (2/3)
Fresh leafy greens: kale, spinach,
lettuce. Root vegetables: carrots.
Introduce gradually to avoid upset.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Rabbit Feed (3/3)
Fresh clean water at all times.
Pelleted feed for balanced nutrition.
Fruits as occasional treats only.
1. Back to menu

Rabbit Prevention (1/3)
Keep cages clean and disinfect
regularly. Quarantine new rabbits
for 2 weeks before introducing.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Rabbit Prevention (2/3)
Check and clean ears regularly
(mite risk). Vaccinate against
Myxomatosis and RHD if available.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Rabbit Prevention (3/3)
Avoid sudden changes to diet.
Ensure rabbits get daily movement
to prevent gut stasis.
1. Back to menu

Rabbit Breeds (1/2)
New Zealand White, California White,
Chinchilla, Flemish Giants.
Local Ugandan, Kabale Breed,
Kenyan White.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Rabbit Breeds (2/2)
Watch for these causes of offspring
death: mother abandoning litter,
cannibalism, insufficient milk,
crushed newborns, weak newborns.
1. Back to menu

Goat Feed (1/3)
Goats need a mix of grass, shrubs
and leaves. Provide dry matter equal
to 3-4% of body weight per day.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Goat Feed (2/3)
Browse plants: Leucaena, Calliandra,
Gliricidia (protein-rich, good for
dry season). Rhodes grass, Guinea
grass, Napier grass.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Goat Feed (3/3)
Crop residues: maize stover, bean
haulms, sweet potato vines.
Provide a salt lick at all times.
Fresh clean water — min 2-3 litres
per adult per day.
1. Back to menu

Goat Care (1/3)
Keep housing dry, clean and
well-ventilated. Raised or slatted
floors help. Separate young kids
from adults at night.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Goat Care (2/3)
Trim hooves every 3-4 months to
prevent lameness. Deworm regularly
— worms are the leading cause of
death in goats in northern Uganda.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Goat Care (3/3)
Check weekly for external parasites:
mange, ticks, lice. Keep sick
animals separate immediately.
1. Back to menu

Goat Prevention (1/4)
Deworm every 3 months. Helminthosis
(worms) is the biggest killer of
goats in this region.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Goat Prevention (2/4)
Vaccinate against Clostridial
diseases annually: Pulpy Kidney,
Blackleg, Tetanus.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Goat Prevention (3/4)
Isolate any animal that aborts
(Brucellosis risk). Quarantine new
animals for 2-3 weeks before mixing.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Goat Prevention (4/4)
Rotate pastures — do not overgraze.
This breaks the worm life cycle.
1. Back to menu

Goat Tick Control (1/2)
Control ticks and mange with
acaricides or dips. Check weekly
for ticks, mange and lice.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Goat Tick Control (2/2)
Ticks spread multiple diseases.
Regular dipping or spraying is
the most effective control method.
1. Back to menu

Goat Breeds (1/3)
Small East African Goat — local,
hardy, good for meat.
Boer x Local cross — improved
meat production.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Goat Breeds (2/3)
Toggenburg/Saanen x Local cross —
improved milk production.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Goat Breeds (3/3)
Introduce buck for 4-6 weeks then
remove. Gestation: ~150 days.
Often have twins — prepare extra
care. Wean kids at 3-4 months.
Do not breed females under 12 months.
1. Back to menu

Sheep Feed (1/3)
Sheep need a mix of grass, shrubs
and leaves. Provide dry matter equal
to 3-4% of body weight per day.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Sheep Feed (2/3)
Browse plants: Leucaena, Calliandra,
Gliricidia. Rhodes grass, Guinea
grass, Napier grass. Crop residues:
maize stover, bean haulms.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Sheep Feed (3/3)
Provide a salt lick at all times.
Phosphorus and calcium important
during pregnancy and lactation.
Mineral blocks are easiest to use.
Fresh clean water always available.
1. Back to menu

Sheep Care (1/3)
Keep housing dry, clean and
well-ventilated. Raised or slatted
floors help. Separate young lambs
from adults at night.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Sheep Care (2/3)
Trim hooves every 3-4 months to
prevent lameness. Deworm regularly
— worms are a leading cause of
death in sheep in northern Uganda.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Sheep Care (3/3)
Check weekly for external parasites:
mange, ticks, lice. Keep sick
animals separate immediately.
1. Back to menu

Sheep Prevention (1/3)
Deworm every 3 months. Vaccinate
against Clostridial diseases
annually: Pulpy Kidney, Blackleg,
Tetanus.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Sheep Prevention (2/3)
Isolate any animal that aborts
(Brucellosis risk). Quarantine new
animals for 2-3 weeks before mixing.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Sheep Prevention (3/3)
Rotate pastures — do not overgraze.
This breaks the worm life cycle.
1. Back to menu

Sheep Tick Control (1/2)
Control ticks and mange with
acaricides or dips. Check weekly
for ticks, mange and lice.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Sheep Tick Control (2/2)
Ticks spread multiple diseases.
Regular dipping or spraying is
the most effective control method.
1. Back to menu

Sheep Breeds (1/2)
Uganda Small East African Sheep
(Nkedi) — local, hardy, suited
to northern Uganda.
Dorper x Local cross — improved
meat breed.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Sheep Breeds (2/2)
Introduce ram for 4-6 weeks then
remove. Gestation: ~147 days.
Often have twins — prepare extra
care. Wean lambs at 3-4 months.
Do not breed females under 12 months.
1. Back to menu

Dog Care (1/4)
Provide clean fresh water every day.
Feed once or twice daily — balanced
diet for the dog's size and age.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Dog Care (2/4)
Good foods: cooked meat scraps,
cooked grains (ugali/posho or rice
mixed with protein), cooked
vegetables like sweet potato,
carrots, pumpkin.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Dog Care (3/4)
Avoid feeding: raw pork or game
meat (parasite risk), onions,
garlic, avocado (toxic to dogs),
chocolate, salty or spiced food.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Dog Care (4/4)
Keep dogs in a clean dry shaded
shelter. Clean up feces regularly.
Keep wounds clean — wash cuts with
clean water. See vet for deep wounds.
1. Back to menu

Dog Prevention (1/3)
Vaccinate against Rabies annually.
Rabies is fatal and can spread
to humans.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Dog Prevention (2/3)
Deworm every 3 months. Treat
regularly for ticks, fleas and mange.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Dog Prevention (3/3)
Isolate any dog showing signs of
illness immediately. Do not allow
dogs to roam freely near wildlife
— increases disease and injury risk.
1. Back to menu

Dog Breeding (1/2)
Wait until female is at least
18 months old before first breeding.
Average pregnancy: 63 days.
Litter size: typically 4-8 puppies.
1. Next
2. Back to menu

Dog Breeding (2/2)
Wean puppies at 6-8 weeks. Keep
mother well-fed and hydrated during
pregnancy and nursing.
1. Back to menu
